methodological_questions: How to define cut-heavy and drive-heavy player roles from play-by-play labels?
How to quantify role travel (performance change when a player changes team or context)?
What statistical methods adjust for team quality and teammate confounding?
What sample size is required to detect a difference in portability between role types?
How reliable are the play-type labels (DRIVE, CUT) in the available data?

historical_evidence.finding: DRIVE PPP is materially higher in regular season (1.198) than playoffs (0.912), a drop of -0.286 across 25 teams, showing DRIVE efficiency is highly context-sensitive.
Play-type label audit FAIL: DRIVE foul-draw rate is 1.7% vs a 14-22% benchmark, indicating systematic misclassification of drive possessions; OTHER class is over 20%.
Apparent DRIVE PPP memory across possessions disappears after within-team demeaning; the global lift is an artifact of team-quality confounding.

A DRIVE-counter comparison with n=44 had an MDE of 0.180 PPP at 80% power, and the observed gap of -0.066 was far below that threshold, demonstrating that small-N play-type comparisons are uninformative.

failed_approaches.why: C_artifact: systematic classification errors, especially DRIVE foul-draw rate far below benchmark, and excessive low-confidence OTHER possessions.

failed_approaches.what_failed: persistent impact score lag curves for DRIVE
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact: global lift disappeared after team-season demeaning; team quality confounded the signal.
A_unanswerable: n=44 gave an MDE of 0.18 PPP, unable to detect a real effect; small sample makes test uninterpretable.

evidence_establishes: DRIVE play-type PPP is context-sensitive (drops sharply in playoff competition).
The current play-type labels, especially DRIVE, have major reliability problems.
DRIVE PPP is confounded by team quality, inflating apparent effects.
Small samples (n~44) cannot support play-type comparisons at plausible effect sizes.
evidence_does_not_establish: Nothing about cut-heavy shapers' role travel or stability across teams.
Nothing about a head-to-head comparison of cut-heavy and drive-heavy role portability.
Whether CUT labels are as unreliable as DRIVE labels.
Any estimate of the sample of players with role changes and their classification as cut-heavy vs drive-heavy.
own_inferences: The n=24 units likely refers to players who changed teams and meet a threshold for cut-heavy or drive-heavy role, which is far below the demonstrated power requirement for play-type comparisons.
If DRIVE labels are unreliable, then classifying 'drive-heavy shapers' will contain substantial measurement error, biasing any comparison toward the null or producing spurious results.
Players who change teams may be selected on recent poor performance, creating a regression-to-the-mean confound that could mimic or mask a travel effect.
Team-offensive-quality confounds play-type PPP; without careful adjustment (e.g., player fixed-effects, opponent-adjusted metrics) any raw comparison of role travel is uninterpretable.
uncertainties: Exact definition of 'shaper' and how it maps to play-type counts or possession shares.
Whether the n=24 refers to distinct players, team-player seasons, or some clustering unit.
Reliability of the CUT label counterpart (not audited in the returned evidence).
Availability and quality of a player role-change sample within the dataset.

historical_effect.explanation: Historical evidence shows that the DRIVE play-type label is fundamentally unreliable (foul-draw rate 1.7% vs 14-22%) and that DRIVE PPP is confounded by team quality, making a classification of 'drive-heavy' shapers untrustworthy. Moreover, prior small-N play-type tests (n=44) were untestable due to low power; the available n=24 is even smaller. These findings shift the assessment from 'uncertain but potentially testable' to 'do not proceed'.

blocking_constraints.text: The DRIVE play-type label has systematic errors (foul-draw rate 1.7% vs benchmark 14-22%); any classification of drive-heavy shapers is severely compromised.
Only n=24 units are available; prior work shows n=44 is insufficient to detect a 0.18 PPP gap for drive-related comparisons.
DRIVE PPP is confounded by team quality; without a validated within-player adjustment model, any travel comparison will reflect team context rather than role portability.

prior_work.summary: No prior study directly tested whether cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones. However, the historical record exposes critical threats: DRIVE labels are unreliable, DRIVE PPP is context-confounded, and small-sample play-type tests are unpowered.

risks.text: DRIVE (and potentially CUT) play-type labels are systematically misclassified, biasing role classification and outcome measurement.
The stated n=24 is too small to detect a realistic effect size; prior work with n=44 failed to distinguish a 0.18 PPP gap.
Team offensive quality and teammate quality confound play-type PPP; without rigorous within-player controls, travel effects will be over- or under-estimated.
Players who change teams may be selected on a down year, inducing regression-to-the-mean that could inflate or obscure travel differences.
The reliability of PPP for low-frequency play types (cuts) in a limited sample of role-change players is unknown and likely low.

design.estimand: Difference in role portability between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers, where portability is the player-level reduction in adjusted PPP variance across team contexts (or the slope of a player's performance vs team-context index).
design.unit: Player-season, with player as the clustering unit for a within-player change analysis.
design.sample: All players with at least 100 possessions of the qualifying play type (CUT or DRIVE) in each of two or more distinct team contexts (different team or same team with materially different roster/coach) from 2022-23 through 2025-26. Need >100 such players; n=24 is insufficient.
design.power: A target of 80% power to detect a difference of 0.05 PPP in portability between groups of ~50 players each, requiring a validated play-type classification and a within-player residual SD of ~0.15 PPP.
design.controls: Team offensive rating, teammate APM proxies, opponent defensive rating, home/away, possession-level contextual features (shot clock, score margin), player usage rate, and player fixed effects.
design.falsification: 1) Audit CUT and DRIVE labels for face validity (foul-draw rates, video spot-checks). 2) Placebo test: randomize play-type assignment within player and check that travel effects disappear. 3) Simulate portability under a null of no true difference using label-randomized data.
design.multiplicity: Pre-specify the single composite portability metric; if sub-group analyses are performed, apply Bonferroni correction for the number of sub-groups.
design.decision_rule: Proceed if the play-type labels pass a new face-validity audit (DRIVE foul-draw > 12%, CUT appropriate), power analysis yields >80% with available n, and a within-player team-context index can be constructed with acceptable fit. Reject the hypothesis if the adjusted portability difference is less than the pre-specified non-inferiority margin (e.g., 0.03 PPP).
design.data_version: Snapshot as of 2026-08-08, using all available regular-season and playoff per-game play-by-play and derived play-type possessions.

methodological_questions: How to define and measure cut-heavy vs drive-heavy player roles from play-by-play data?
How to quantify role travel/portability across teams and seasons?
What statistical methods address confounding in player role comparisons across different contexts?
What sample size and data requirements exist to detect differences in role portability?
What are known confounders when comparing off-ball and on-ball player roles?
args.query: cut-heavy shapers roles travel better than drive-heavy ones portability of player roles across teams

Research question (as posed on 2026-08-08, in the area of structural roles and influence):
Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["cut-heavy shapers", "drive-heavy shapers", "role portability", "role travel", "off-ball movement", "driving", "player role transferability", "structural roles", "influence"], "methodological_questions": ["How to define and measure cut-heavy vs drive-heavy player roles from play-by-play data?", "How to quantify role travel/portability across teams and seasons?", "What statistical methods address confounding in player role comparisons across different contexts?", "What sample size and data requirements exist to detect differences in role portability?", "What are known confounders when comparing off-ball and on-ball player roles?"], "query": "cut-heavy shapers roles travel better than drive-heavy ones portability of player roles across teams"}}

reasoning_details.text:
We need to identify research concepts and methodological questions from the research question: "Cut-heavy shapers' roles travel better than drive-heavy ones."

Interpretation: This likely refers to basketball. "Cut-heavy shapers" probably refers to players whose role is characterized by cutting (off-ball movement to the basket, receiving passes for finishes). "Drive-heavy ones" refers to players who rely on driving to the basket with the ball. "Roles travel better" likely means that a player's role (their offensive style, perhaps measured by metrics like role consistency or effectiveness) is more transferable across teams or contexts for cut-heavy shapers compared to drive-heavy shapers. So the question is about the transferability or consistency of player role/effectiveness when moving from one team to another or from one season to the next? "Travel" could also mean that the role's effectiveness is more invariant across defensive schemes? Need to parse carefully. Possibly from a "structural roles and influence" area, so it's about how player role types (shapers) influence outcomes, and whether cut-heavy ones are more "traveling" (i.e., their impact or role definition is more stable across team contexts) than drive-heavy ones. Might be about on/off-court influence, or about role portability when players change teams.

Given the context, I should define research concepts: "cut-heavy shapers", "drive-heavy shapers", "role travel" (i.e., portability, consistency across contexts), "structural roles", "influence". Also methodological questions: how to define "shaper", "cut-heavy", "drive-heavy", how to measure "role travel" (e.g., consistency of role metrics like usage, efficiency, play-type frequency across teams/lineups), how to handle confounding (e.g., player skill, team system, sample size). Also data: play-by-play, play-type possession records, defensive matchups, etc. So I'll craft a query that asks for prior research on cut-heavy vs drive-heavy players and role portability.

Then I'll call retrieve_history with these concepts and questions. Must be JSON with list of strings for research_concepts and methodological_questions, and a query string. So I'll output that.
